meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing'?
meta.ogDescription: Archilochus wrote it; Isaiah Berlin's 1953 essay gave it this English wording; Jim Collins borrowed it for Good to Great — and says so himself.

answer.label: Not Jim Collins — actually Archilochus
answer.authorDates: c. 680 – c. 645 BC · Greek iambic poet of Paros · this English wording from Isaiah Berlin, 1953
answer.sourceLine: The line is Archilochus, fragment 201 — and the exact English sentence people quote is the one at the head of Isaiah Berlin’s 1953 essay The Hedgehog and the Fox, which opens by naming Archilochus outright. Jim Collins borrowed it for the “Hedgehog Concept” in Good to Great (2001) and credits Berlin and “an ancient Greek parable” on his own site ↗.

source.excerpt: There is a line among the fragments of the Greek poet Archilochus which says: ‘The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing.’
trail: 7th century BC — Archilochus composes the line; it survives only as a fragment, listed at fragment 201 among his sourced quotes ↗.

1931 — J. M. Edmonds renders it for the Loeb Elegy and Iambus, Volume II as “The Fox knoweth many things, the Hedgehog one great thing ↗,” citing Zenobius — recognisably the same line, not the famous wording.

1953 — Isaiah Berlin opens The Hedgehog and the Fox with the sentence in the form the world now quotes, naming Archilochus in the same breath ↗. The essay had appeared in shorter form as “Lev Tolstoy’s Historical Scepticism” in Oxford Slavonic Papers 2 (1951) ↗.
2001 — Jim Collins makes it the seed of the “Hedgehog Concept” in Good to Great, introducing it as Berlin’s use of an ancient Greek parable ↗ — after which the internet begins crediting Collins.
source.excerptNote: The first sentence of Berlin’s essay. Its footnote sends the reader to the Greek — fragment 201 in M. L. West’s Iambi et Elegi Graeci — and, in the second edition, adds an editorial note on Zenobius and the rival Homeric claim.

source.rightsNote: Archilochus’ Greek is ancient and free of copyright, but this English sentence is the one printed in Berlin’s essay, first published in 1953 by Weidenfeld and Nicolson — comfortably inside US copyright, and still in print in Princeton’s second edition, edited by Henry Hardy. Quoting the line with attribution is ordinary fair use; reprinting Berlin’s essay is not, and the older Loeb wording by J. M. Edmonds (1931) is a separate rights question of its own.

author.name: Archilochus
author.heading: Who Archilochus was
author.metaLine: c. 680 – c. 645 BC · Greek iambic poet from Paros
author.bio: Archilochus was a Greek poet from the island of Paros in the Archaic period, celebrated as the earliest known Greek author to compose almost entirely on the theme of his own emotions and experiences. His complete works are lost: what survives is roughly three hundred fragments plus about forty paraphrases and indirect quotations, many of them recovered from damaged Egyptian papyri or preserved only because a later writer quoted them. The fox-and-hedgehog line is one of those — seven Greek words that outlived every poem they came from.

misattribution.heading: Why Jim Collins gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Nobody faked this one. It drifted onto Collins’ name because Good to Great put it in front of millions of readers who had never read a 1953 essay on Tolstoy — and quote sites followed the traffic.

items.why: Collins built the “Hedgehog Concept” on the line in Good to Great (HarperCollins, 2001), but his own site frames it plainly: “In his famous essay ‘The Hedgehog and the Fox,’ Isaiah Berlin divided the world into hedgehogs and foxes, based upon an ancient Greek parable” ↗.

Berlin’s essay is where this exact phrasing entered general circulation, and it is often quoted under his name for that reason — but his very first sentence hands it back: “There is a line among the fragments of the Greek poet Archilochus” ↗.

The editorial note in Princeton’s second edition records that Zenobius, who preserved the line, “says that it is found in both Archilochus and Homer,” and reasons that the iambic metre points instead to the pseudo-Homeric Margites, probably later than Archilochus’ poem ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Archilochus, fragment 201 ↗; the English sentence everyone quotes is the one printed at the head of Isaiah Berlin’s 1953 essay; Jim Collins is the third owner of a very old idea.

context.heading: How an Archaic Greek fragment became a management slogan
lead: Berlin’s essay is the hinge. It began as a journal article, “Lev Tolstoy’s Historical Scepticism,” in Oxford Slavonic Papers 2 (1951) ↗, and was expanded into the book The Hedgehog and the Fox: An Essay on Tolstoy’s View of History, published in 1953 by Weidenfeld and Nicolson in London and Simon and Schuster in New York. Berlin used the fragment to split thinkers into two kinds — those who relate everything to one central vision, and those who chase many unrelated ends — and then spent the rest of the essay asking which one Tolstoy was.

Half a century later Jim Collins made the same animals do corporate work. Good to Great (HarperCollins, 2001) turned “hedgehog” into a strategy test: find the one thing you can be best in the world at and drive at it. The framing travelled so far that the sentence itself now gets pinned on Collins — which is a little unfair to him, since he opens the idea by handing the credit to Berlin.
context.detailsSummary: The ancient paper trail, and the other English wordings
detailsBody: The fragment survives because a proverb collector wrote it down. The editorial note in Princeton’s second edition records that it “was preserved in a collection of proverbs by the Greek Sophist Zenobius (5. 68), who says that it is found in both Archilochus and Homer,” and argues that because the line is iambic rather than dactylic in metre, the Homeric attribution likely points to the pseudo-Homeric comic epic Margites — probably later than Archilochus’ poem. See the essay’s opening page and footnote ↗.

Berlin’s is not the only English version. J. M. Edmonds, translating the fragment for Elegy and Iambus, Volume II (Harvard University Press / William Heinemann, 1931), gives it as “The Fox knoweth many things, the Hedgehog one great thing ↗,” citing Zenobius. Wikiquote also lists “the fox knows many tricks; the hedgehog one good one.” It is Berlin’s phrasing, not any of these, that Collins and everyone after him quotes.

Later writers kept reusing the animals and quietly changing the verdict. A 2023 essay in Antigone traces how Philip Tetlock and others reinterpreted Berlin’s metaphor, often reversing his judgements about which animal comes out ahead ↗ — Collins’ pro-hedgehog reading is one move in a long argument, not the original meaning.
context.pull: Seven Greek words, quoted by a proverb collector, borrowed by an Oxford philosopher, and eventually printed on a strategy slide.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the fox/hedgehog line among Archilochus' sourced quotes as fragment 201, gives the Greek, offers variant translations ('the fox knows many things; the hedgehog one great thing'; 'the fox knows many tricks; the hedgehog one good one'), and notes it was quoted in The Hedgehog and the Fox (1953) by Isaiah Berlin.

Berlin's essay opens: 'There is a line among the fragments of the Greek poet Archilochus which says: "The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing."' The footnote cites Archilochus fragment 201 in M. L. West (ed.), Iambi et elegi graeci ante Alexandrum cantati, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Oxford, 1989), and an editorial note records that the fragment was preserved by Zenobius (5.68), who says it is found in both Archilochus and Homer, with the iambic metre pointing to the pseudo-Homeric Margites.

Jim Collins' own site says: 'In his famous essay "The Hedgehog and the Fox," Isaiah Berlin divided the world into hedgehogs and foxes, based upon an ancient Greek parable: "The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing."' — i.e. Collins credits Berlin, not himself.

The essay was first published as 'Lev Tolstoy's Historical Scepticism' in Oxford Slavonic Papers 2 (1951), 17–54, and expanded as The Hedgehog and the Fox: An Essay on Tolstoy's View of History (London: Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 1953; New York: Simon and Schuster, 1953).

J. M. Edmonds' translation in Elegy and Iambus, Volume II (Harvard University Press / William Heinemann, 1931) renders the fragment 'The Fox knoweth many things, the Hedgehog one great thing,' citing Zenobius' Proverbs.

Archilochus lived c. 680 – c. 645 BC, came from Paros, was an iambic poet described as the earliest known Greek author to compose almost entirely on the theme of his own emotions and experiences, and his work survives only in roughly three hundred fragments plus about forty paraphrases or indirect quotations.

The Hedgehog and the Fox was published as a book in 1953 by Weidenfeld & Nicolson; the fragment is numbered 103 in the Diehl edition and 201 in the West edition, with the Greek printed as πόλλ' οἶδ' ἀλώπηξ, ἀλλ' ἐχῖνος ἓν μέγα.

Princeton University Press's edition is a second edition, edited by Henry Hardy, published 2 June 2013, and its description quotes the line as 'This ancient Greek aphorism, preserved in a fragment from the poet Archilochus.'

Good to Great was published in 2001 by HarperCollins, authored by Jim Collins, and its 'hedgehog concept' draws on Isaiah Berlin's essay 'The Hedgehog and the Fox' and the ancient Greek parable summarised by this line.

This classics essay discusses Archilochus fragment 201, the ancient commentator Zenobius, and how later authors including Tetlock reinterpreted Berlin's fox/hedgehog metaphor, often reversing his judgements about which animal succeeds.
